Florida Sues Sweepstakes Casino Giants VGW and Stake Over "Illegal Gambling" Claims

Published August 20, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has filed lawsuits against sweepstakes casino operators VGW and Stake, arguing that their "free-to-play" model is illegal gambling dressed up in a legal costume. Four payment processors that support the platforms — Breeze Labs, Praxis, Trustly, and Worldpay — are also named as defendants, along with Stake co-founders Ed Craven and Bijan Tehrani individually.

The core argument: two currencies, one product

Sweepstakes casinos operate on a dual-currency system: players get "Gold Coins," which have no cash value and can be played for fun, alongside "Sweeps Coins," which can be redeemed for real cash prizes. Operators have long argued this structure keeps them outside the legal definition of gambling in most states, since no purchase is technically required to obtain Sweeps Coins.

Uthmeier's complaint rejects that framing outright. He contends the dual-currency setup is a legal fiction that functions the same as selling casino chips for cash, just under a different name. In comments accompanying the filing, he put it bluntly: "If it looks, swims, and quacks like a duck, it's a duck" — describing the sweepstakes model as a "gateway drug" to real-money gambling that pushes consumers down a "dark alley" into unregulated territory.

What Florida is asking for

The lawsuits seek to shut down VGW's and Stake's sweepstakes-casino operations in Florida, recover what the state characterizes as illegal gambling proceeds, secure restitution for consumers, and impose civil penalties. Notably, Uthmeier's office argues no new legislation is needed to pursue this — it says Florida's existing gambling statutes already cover the sweepstakes model. A separate bill that would have specifically targeted sweepstakes casinos died in committee in the Florida legislature earlier this year.

Part of a wider pattern

Florida isn't acting alone. Multiple states have passed anti-sweepstakes legislation since 2025, and Kentucky's attorney general brought similar action against the same category of operators before Florida's filing. The sweepstakes casino sector — which has grown quickly by offering casino-style games in states where real-money online casino gambling remains illegal or unlicensed — is increasingly a target for state regulators and legislators nationwide.

For players, the practical takeaway is the same one we give anywhere the legal status of an operator is disputed: platforms operating in a legal gray area carry real risk, including the possibility that withdrawals, balances, or the platform itself could be disrupted by regulatory action with little notice. Our casino guides stick to games and operators licensed under standard real-money regulatory frameworks for that reason.
